data.title: [burn-nn] Convolutions: support asymmetric padding w/ `Same`
Automatically detect and test backend kernel overrides in Dispatch
data.body:
### Feature Description

Ensure backend kernel overrides, like `ctc_loss`, are automatically registered and properly tested. Right now, tests may only hit the default implementation if a backend-specific override is missing, so backend kernels can go untested, missing bugs until later.

### Why This Matters
- Tests might pass even if a fused backend kernel (e.g., cubecl) isn't called.
- Missing overrides mean some errors are only found at runtime.
- Adding or changing ops/traits (like `softmax` or `layer_norm`) increases this risk.

### Possible Solutions
- Automate backend override registration (e.g., using crates like inventory).
- Add CI checks or linter warnings for missing overrides when traits are updated.
- Eventually, consider a macro to automate trait method wiring; for now, require manual registration but notify maintainers when updates are needed.

---
**Tag:** automation, dispatch, test coverage

data.title: Add MaxPool3d module (3D max pooling)
data.body:
Burn currently lacks a native 3D max pooling module (`MaxPool3d`), whereas 1D and 2D max pooling modules are provided as `MaxPool1d` and `MaxPool2d`. This blocks full 3D CNN support and disables relevant ONNX tests (see https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/pull/355).

**Requested feature:**
- Implement a `MaxPool3d` module in line with the existing 1D/2D modules, following the same API and semantics as PyTorch and ONNX.
- Include options for kernel size, stride, padding, dilation, ceil_mode, etc., to cover common 3D pooling use cases and enable ONNX compatibility.
- Add comprehensive tests and documentation.

**Motivation:**
- 3D convolutional architectures require efficient 3D max pooling for tasks in medical imaging, video, and volumetric data.
- Essential for parity with other frameworks and for passing ONNX test suites with 3D models.

Reference: [burn-onnx#343](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/issues/343) and related backend skips.

data.title: Add AvgPool3d module (3D average pooling)
data.body:
Burn currently lacks a native 3D average pooling module (`AvgPool3d`), while `AvgPool1d` and `AvgPool2d` are available. Full 3D pooling support is needed for volumetric data and models such as 3D U-Net used in medical imaging or video processing. The ONNX importer, as of https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/pull/355, points to this limitation with clear panics and disables several backend tests pending implementation. 

**Requested feature:**
- Implement `AvgPool3d` module in burn-nn, mirroring the API and behavior of the 1D and 2D variants.
- Include configuration of kernel size, stride, padding (possibly asymmetric & "same"), dilation, ceil_mode, and count_include_pad where applicable, matching ONNX/torch semantics.
- Add tests and documentation.

**Motivation:**
- Support 3D CNNs (e.g. medical, volumetric, video models) in Burn.
- Enable ONNX models and tests relying on 3D pooling.

Reference: [burn-onnx#343](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/issues/343) and tests marked `skip-codegen` for 3D pool ops.

data.title: Fusion stream cascade: task panic floods log with ordering.rs index-out-of-bounds noise
data.body:
## Summary

When a task fails inside a `burn-fusion` stream (panic, error, anything), the stream's execution state becomes corrupted and all subsequent operations on the same stream panic at [`burn-fusion/src/stream/execution/ordering.rs:65`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/main/crates/burn-fusion/src/stream/execution/ordering.rs#L65) with `index out of bounds: the len is N but the index is N`.

The original failure then gets buried under ~30 identical cascading panics, making the real root cause very hard to find. When I first hit this I spent significant time looking in the wrong place (`ordering.rs`) before tracing back to find the actual panic was elsewhere (in our case, a cubecl `FastDivmod` divide-by-zero — tracked in [tracel-ai/cubecl#1296](https://github.com/tracel-ai/cubecl/issues/1296) / [#1297](https://github.com/tracel-ai/cubecl/pull/1297)).

## Observed output (trimmed)

```
thread 'Device-4-0' panicked at cubecl-std/src/fast_math.rs:79:22:
    attempt to divide by zero            # ← real root cause, fires ONCE

[2026-04-17T00:12:32Z WARN  cubecl_common::device::handle::channel::task] Task failed: Any { .. }

thread 'Device-4-0' panicked at burn-fusion/src/stream/execution/ordering.rs:65:38:
    index out of bounds: the len is 1 but the index is 1
thread 'Device-4-0' panicked at burn-fusion/src/stream/execution/ordering.rs:65:38:
    index out of bounds: the len is 1 but the index is 1
... [repeats ~30x, drowning the log] ...
thread 'Device-4-0' panicked at burn-fusion/src/stream/execution/ordering.rs:65:38:
    index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0

thread 'full_pipeline_test' panicked at burn-fusion/src/client.rs:153:14:
    called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: CallError
```

## Root cause

`execute_operations` at `ordering.rs:65` iterates `ordering: &[usize]` and indexes `self.operations[*id]`. When an earlier task panicked, its entries were not cleaned up properly before the next task tried to execute, so `ordering` contains IDs that are no longer valid for `operations`. Each subsequent task fires the same panic.

## Minimal repro

Any panic inside a Fusion stream task will trigger this cascade. For a concrete repro:

1. Apply any patch that makes a cubecl kernel panic (easiest: revert my cubecl fix #1297 and run Brush 3DGS training with `refine()` enabled on a small dataset on Metal — `FastDivmod::new(0)` panics at the first refine).
2. Observe: one real panic, followed by ~30 identical `ordering.rs:65` panics, followed by a generic `CallError` unwrap on the main thread.

## Impact

- Debugging burden: real cause hidden under cascade noise.
- Downstream users (Brush, us, anyone building on burn with fusion enabled) see 30+ stacks and assume burn-fusion is the bug, when it's actually an error-propagation issue.

## Suggested fix

When a task panics (or returns `Err`) during Fusion stream execution:

1. Mark the stream as poisoned / drain remaining operations without trying to execute them.
2. Propagate the **original** error back to the caller via `client.rs:153`, not a generic `CallError`.
3. Subsequent ops on a poisoned stream should short-circuit with a meaningful "stream previously failed with: ..." error, not try to index a corrupted vec.

Something along the lines of wrapping the body of `execute_operations` in a catch_unwind or checking `id < self.operations.len()` with an early-return + one-shot log would at least stop the cascade. Properly propagating the first error would be the cleaner fix.

## Environment

- Hardware: Apple M4, macOS 26.3
- Backend: wgpu Metal
- Rust: 1.94.0
- burn: `965a59ec` (main, 2026-04-16)
- cubecl: `34625c91`
- Brush: `83b7c71f` (main, triggered this in the wild)

## Context

Happy to submit a PR if you have a preferred direction for the fix (poisoned-stream flag vs. `catch_unwind` vs. bounds-check early-return). Let me know.

data.title: Int remainder is inconsistently wrong on Wgpu backend
burn-fusion adds too much overhead even with all optimizations disabled
data.body:
## Summary

With burn-fusion layered on top of burn-cubecl, we observe a ~40% slowdown on model inference compared to running burn-cubecl directly — even with all fusion optimizations disabled and the exact same kernels executing. The fusion layer should be a zero-cost abstraction when it's not optimizing anything. This issue tracks investigating the source of the overhead and eliminating it.

## Measurements

- **Workload**: transformer block inference, 62 kernels.
- **Without fusion**: ~800 µs end-to-end.
- **With fusion (no optimizations)**: ~1.2 ms end-to-end.
- **Overhead**: ~400 µs / ~40%, spread across 62 kernels (~6.5 µs per kernel of pure framework tax).

This is with fusion optimizations disabled, meaning the fusion layer is doing nothing useful — it receives operations, doesn't fuse or reorder them, and forwards the same kernels to the CubeCL runtime. The overhead is entirely framework machinery.

## Goal

Adding the burn-fusion layer to burn-cubecl should not add measurable overhead. With optimizations disabled, GPU utilization should be identical to running without fusion. The fusion layer's bookkeeping cost per kernel must be negligible relative to kernel execution time.

## Investigation areas

The source of the overhead is not yet identified. The following are areas to profile and investigate (not exhaustive):

- **Channel overhead**: the device channel is now non-blocking with thread-local recursive execution (no longer a reentrant mutex). However, the message passing, thread-local dispatch, and any serialization involved in routing operations through the channel could still add per-operation cost.
- **IR construction and traversal**: even with optimizations disabled, the fusion layer may still be building its intermediate representation for each operation before deciding there's nothing to optimize. If the IR is allocated and discarded every time, that's allocation churn on the hot path.
- **Handle reference counting / cloning**: fusion wraps tensor handles in its own tracking layer. Extra reference count operations (clone, drop, Arc overhead) on every tensor for every operation could be significant at µs-scale kernel granularity.
- **Context management**: the fusion global context tracks operation state, pending operations, and streams. Updating this bookkeeping per-operation may be expensive.
- **Redundant dispatching**: the path from "fusion receives an operation" to "CubeCL executes the kernel" may involve extra indirection, trait dispatch, or serialization steps that don't exist in the direct burn-cubecl path.
- **Memory management interactions**: fusion may trigger extra memory management work (e.g. checking if buffers can be reused, updating metadata) that the direct path avoids.

## Approach

1. **Profile**: instrument the fusion hot path (operation registration → decision → kernel dispatch) with fine-grained timing to identify where the ~6.5 µs per-kernel overhead is spent.
2. **Compare code paths**: trace a single kernel's execution through both the fusion and non-fusion paths to identify every extra step the fusion layer introduces.
3. **Fix**: eliminate or defer the expensive steps. For operations that won't be optimized, the fusion layer should be as close to a pass-through as possible.

data.title: Add complex-to-complex FFT (fft / ifft) to signal module
data.body:
## Summary

Add `fft` and `ifft` (complex-to-complex) to `burn::tensor::signal`, alongside the existing `rfft` / `irfft` (real-to-complex).

## Motivation

`burn::tensor::signal` currently provides only real FFT variants:
- `rfft`: real input → complex output (onesided)
- `irfft`: complex input (onesided) → real output

This is enough for most audio use cases, but the ONNX [`DFT`](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__DFT.html) operator requires two more behaviors that the real variants can't express:

1. **Complex-to-complex forward DFT** — when the ONNX input has trailing dim = 2 (interleaved real/imag), the operator is defined as a full complex FFT. Not a superset of `rfft`; the input is already complex.
2. **Inverse DFT** — ONNX's `inverse=1` is the complex-to-complex inverse FFT. It is not the same as `irfft`: `irfft` assumes onesided complex input with conjugate symmetry and returns a real signal, whereas ONNX IDFT takes full complex input and returns full complex output.

As a result, burn-onnx's DFT implementation explicitly rejects both cases (see the error messages in [`dft.rs`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/blob/main/crates/onnx-ir/src/node/dft.rs) — "Burn's irfft is the inverse of rfft (onesided real FFT), which differs from ONNX's complex-to-complex inverse DFT" and "complex-to-complex DFT is not supported by Burn's current signal API"). Any ONNX model that round-trips through the frequency domain or that passes complex tensors through DFT is currently unconvertible.

This is blocking full DFT support in burn-onnx (see tracel-ai/burn-onnx#161).

## Proposed API

Mirror the existing `rfft` signature but accept and return complex-encoded tensors (trailing dim = 2 for real/imag):

```rust
/// Forward complex FFT along `axis`.
///
/// Input:  [..., N, ..., 2] — real/imag pair in the trailing dim.
/// Output: [..., N, ..., 2] — same shape; frequency bins in `axis`.
pub fn fft<B: Backend, const D: usize>(
    input: Tensor<B, D>,
    axis: usize,
) -> Tensor<B, D>;

/// Inverse complex FFT along `axis`.
///
/// Input:  [..., N, ..., 2]
/// Output: [..., N, ..., 2]
pub fn ifft<B: Backend, const D: usize>(
    input: Tensor<B, D>,
    axis: usize,
) -> Tensor<B, D>;
```

Alternative: take two tensors (real and imaginary) and return two tensors, to avoid the trailing-dim convention. Either is fine as long as it's consistent with how `rfft`/`irfft` will be aligned with it.

## Reference behavior

- torch.fft.fft: <https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.fft.fft.html>
- torch.fft.ifft: <https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.fft.ifft.html>
- ONNX DFT spec: <https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__DFT.html>
- numpy.fft.fft / numpy.fft.ifft

## Implementation sketch

Since `rfft` already exists, `fft` can likely be built on top of it for correctness first, then specialized later. For a real input with zero imaginary part, `fft(x + 0i) == [rfft_output, mirrored_conjugate]`. For general complex input, decompose into `fft(re + i·im) = fft(re) + i·fft(im)` and combine using the identity that lets you compute two real FFTs as one complex FFT. Or just call the backend's native complex FFT routines where available (cuFFT, Accelerate, etc.).

`ifft(x) = conj(fft(conj(x))) / N` is the classic correctness-preserving implementation when the forward exists.

## Out of scope

- 2D/ND convenience wrappers (`fft2`, `fftn`) — can be follow-ups
- Real-valued specializations beyond what `rfft`/`irfft` already cover

## Related

- tracel-ai/burn-onnx#161 — ONNX signal operators; this unblocks complex and inverse DFT paths
- tracel-ai/burn#4782 — companion request for STFT
- tracel-ai/burn#4783 — companion request for BlackmanWindow

data.title: Add mel spectrogram to burn-tensor signal module
data.body:
## Summary

Now that `rfft`, `irfft`, and `hamming_window` are available, burn has all the building blocks to implement mel spectrogram as a high-level signal processing operation.

## Motivation

Mel spectrograms are the standard input representation for audio ML models (Whisper, wav2vec2, HiFi-GAN, EnCodec, etc.). Currently users would need to manually compose the pipeline from lower-level ops. A built-in `mel_spectrogram` would make audio models first-class in Burn.

## Proposed API

```rust
use burn_tensor::signal;

// Forward: audio -> mel spectrogram
let mel = signal::mel_spectrogram(audio, MelSpectrogramOptions {
    sample_rate: 16000,
    n_fft: 400,          // window size (power of 2)
    hop_length: 160,     // stride between frames
    n_mels: 80,          // number of mel bands
    window: WindowType::Hann,
});

// Inverse (approximate): mel spectrogram -> audio
let audio = signal::inverse_mel_spectrogram(mel, ...);
```

## Implementation

All components exist as tensor ops today:

| Step | Operation | Status |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Sliding windows | `unfold` | Available |
| Window function | `hamming_window` | Available (#4698) |
| Forward FFT | `rfft` | Available (#4707) |
| Power spectrum | element-wise `pow(2)` + `add` | Available |
| Mel filterbank | `matmul` with precomputed filter matrix | Available |
| Log scaling | `log` | Available |
| Inverse FFT | `irfft` | Available (#4719) |

The main new code needed:
1. **Mel filterbank matrix construction** - triangular filters spaced on the mel scale
2. **STFT / ISTFT** - compose unfold + window + rfft (and inverse)
3. **`mel_spectrogram`** - compose STFT + power spectrum + mel filterbank + log

This could live in `burn-tensor/src/tensor/signal/` alongside the existing `fft.rs`.

## Prior Art

- PyTorch: `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram`
- TensorFlow: `tf.signal.stft` + `tf.signal.linear_to_mel_weight_matrix`
- Python: `librosa.feature.melspectrogram`

data.title: Bug: Non-Contiguous Layer Indices remapping causes incorrect weights mapping in PytorchStore
data.body:
**Describe the bug**
PytorchStore's "Non-Contiguous Layer Indices" feature appears to incorrectly remap certain weights when loading a model with non-contiguous indices, resulting in parameter name mismatches. Error messages are produced when loading models, e.g.:

- model_g.flow.flows.4.enc.in_layers.0.bias
    Did you mean: 'model_g.flow.flows.1.enc.in_layers.0.bias'?
- model_g.flow.flows.4.enc.in_layers.0.weight_g
    Did you mean: 'model_g.flow.flows.1.enc.in_layers.0.weight_g'?

Reported by a Discord user (see [reference](https://discord.com/channels/1038839012602941528/1059209073784008835/1489262642911645847)).

Model weights are named, for example:
model_g.flow.flows.0.pre.weight [192, 96, 1]
model_g.flow.flows.0.pre.bias [192]
model_g.flow.flows.0.enc.in_layers.0.bias [384]
model_g.flow.flows.0.enc.in_layers.0.weight_g [384, 1, 1]
model_g.flow.flows.2.pre.weight [192, 96, 1]
model_g.flow.flows.2.pre.bias [192]
model_g.flow.flows.2.enc.in_layers.0.bias [384]
model_g.flow.flows.2.enc.in_layers.0.weight_g [384, 1, 1]

The weights for flows 1 and 3 are missing, and remapping appears to be introducing errors when corresponding Burn weight indices do not match PyTorch's non-contiguous order.

Users have confirmed that disabling the `map_indices_contiguous` flag leads to other mismatches, so the default mapping *should* work but currently doesn't handle gaps as intended.

**To Reproduce**
1. Load a PyTorch model with non-contiguous layer indices (e.g., a model with flows 0, 2, 4 but missing 1 and 3 in `model_g.flow.flows`)
2. Attempt to import into Burn using PytorchStore with default or enabled `map_indices_contiguous`
3. Observe parameter mismatch errors in log (see above for example)

**Expected behavior**
The remapping of non-contiguous PyTorch indices should correctly assign weights so that all available weights from PyTorch are mapped to the expected Burn model parameters, with no missing or misassigned tensors.

**Additional context**
- [Discord bug discussion](https://discord.com/channels/1038839012602941528/1059209073784008835/1489262642911645847)
- Possibly a logical error in the remapping function when PyTorch indices are non-contiguous.
- See Burn documentation: "Non-Contiguous Layer Indices"

Broken sizes (max_diff ~1.0): 214, 218, 220, 227, 230, 235, 242, 245, 255 Working sizes (max_diff = 0.0): 200, 210, 212, 216, 224, 240, 256 Minimal reproduction: https://github.com/wkrettek/burn-interpolate-repro **Expected behavior** Ndarray and Wgpu backends should produce the same output. **Screenshots** **Desktop (please complete the following information):** - OS: CachyOS - RTX 3080 Ti - Version Burn 0.20.1, cubecl 0.9.0 - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti, driver 595.58.03, Vulkan 1.4.341 - Linux 6.19.10 **Additional context** **Root cause** The nearest-neighbor kernel in crates/burn-cubecl/src/kernel/interpolate/nearest.rs uses f32 arithmetic to map output coordinates to input coordinates: let y = y as f32 * (h_in / h_out); let x = x as f32 * (w_in / w_out); For certain dimension pairs, the GPU's f32 division produces a result that lands just below an integer boundary. data.title: Reshaping block quantized tensors on wgpu backend loses data
data.body:
**Describe the bug**

Taking a quantized tensor and reshaping it loses data. For example, reshaping a `[32]` tensor into `[2, 32]` sets the second half of the elements to zero.

This is probably related to using `QuantLevel::block([32])` as using `16` (or lower numbers) or `QuantLevel::Tensor` solves it.
See also further comments in the code example next to the quant scheme.

Transposing the quantized tensor in addition sets all elements to zero, which might make all this related to https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/issues/4491

Note that this is with latest git main as of now (7c3be3be027645026e41c29233d8a089d5a28ef8) but also happens with the latest stable release.

**To Reproduce**

```rust
fn main() {
    let device = Default::default();

    let rows = 2;
    let cols = 16;

        .map(|i| (i as f32) / n_elements as f32)

data.title: Implement Pinball/Quantile Regression Loss
data.body:
### Feature description

Pinball/Quantile loss is a regression loss used to estimate conditional quantiles of a target distribution instead of its mean. It thus introduces asymmetric penalties for under- and overprediction. This allows a model to directly infer prediction bounds, such as the 5th and 95th percentiles. Applications include uncertainty estimation or anomaly detection, e.g., see the article in [1].

Definition:
```
For multiple quantiles q_1, ..., q_n, the pinball loss can be defined as

L(y, ŷ) = (1 / n) * Σ_i max(q_i * (y - ŷ_{q_i}), (q_i - 1) * (y - ŷ_{q_i}))

where ŷ_{q_i} is the prediction for quantile q_i.

Equivalent form:

L_i = q_i * relu(y - ŷ_{q_i}) + (1 - q_i) * relu(ŷ_{q_i} - y)
```

### Feature motivation

This loss function is commonly used for uncertainty estimation, risk-sensitive forecasting, and (unsupervised) anomaly detection. I needed it for a project, and I believe it's a good contribution to this repository, as it often gets overlooked.

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

As already stated, I have this **essentially ready for PR (needs rebase) if the feature is accepted** from a previous project.
Essentially implements the following:
- loss and associated tests in `burn/crates/burn-nn/src/loss/pinball.rs`
- an example for anomaly detection using the UCI Wine Quality dataset.
- updated table in burn-book

### Sources

data.title: Tensor::expand should support ONNX/numpy max-semantics for shape dimensions
Panic during training, burn-ir/handle.rs
data.body:
---                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  ## Bug: `no_grad()` embedding parameters crash training at epoch boundary on wgpu/fusion backend                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
  **burn version:** 0.20.1                                                                                                                                                                                                   
  **backend:** `Autodiff<Fusion<WgpuRuntime>>`                                                                                                                                                                               
  **crate:** `burn-ir`, `burn-train`                                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
  ---                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
  ### Description                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
  When an `Embedding` layer is frozen with `.no_grad()` and the model is trained with
  `SupervisedTraining` + `with_file_checkpointer`, training panics at the start of the
  **third epoch** (iteration 1–2) with:

  panicked at burn-ir-0.20.1/src/handle.rs:88:
  Should have handle for tensor TensorId { value: ... }

  This causes the async checkpointer thread to receive a `SendError` on its channel,
  which then panics again in its destructor, producing a double-panic abort:

  panicked at async_checkpoint.rs:123: Can send message to checkpointer thread.
  panicked at async_checkpoint.rs:162: Can send the end message to the checkpointer thread.
  panicked at panicking.rs:233: panic in a destructor during cleanup
  Aborted (core dumped)

  The failure is **100% reproducible** and always triggers at the same point: the first
  training iteration after epoch 2's validation + checkpoint.

  ---

  ### Root cause

  `get_handle` in `burn-ir` has two code paths for the `TensorStatus`:

  ```rust
  TensorStatus::ReadOnly  => { self.handles.insert(id, Handle::Existing(handle.clone())); handle }
  TensorStatus::ReadWrite => handle  // ← handle is consumed; NOT re-inserted

  When SupervisedTraining saves a checkpoint after epoch 2 validation, the async
  checkpointer serialises the model's parameters to disk. For a no_grad() embedding,
  this involves a ReadWrite drain of the weight tensor's GPU buffer — which
  removes the handle from the map and does not re-insert it.

  Because the embedding has require_grad = false, the fusion backend considers the
  tensor "done" after this drain: it is not referenced in any pending autodiff graph
  and will not be needed for a backward pass. The handle is therefore not
  re-registered.

  When epoch 3 starts and embedding.forward() is dispatched to the fusion backend,
  it looks up the embedding weight's TensorId — which is no longer in the handle
  map — and panics.

  The sequence in the experiment log confirms this precisely:

  Executing validation step for epoch 2   ← epoch 2 validation runs fine
  Executing training step for epoch 3
  Iteration 1
  ERROR: panicked … Should have handle for tensor TensorId { value: … }

  ---
  Minimal reproduction

  // model with frozen GloVe embedding
  let embedding = EmbeddingConfig::new(vocab_size, embed_dim)
      .init(device)
      .no_grad();               // ← triggers the bug

  // train with file checkpointer on wgpu backend
  SupervisedTraining::new(dir, train_loader, val_loader)
      .with_file_checkpointer(CompactRecorder::new())
      .num_epochs(10)
      .launch(learner);
  // → panics at start of epoch 3

  ---
  Why no_grad() triggers this but regular params don't

  For a parameter with require_grad = true, the fusion backend keeps the handle
  alive because it expects the tensor to participate in a future backward pass (the
  handle will be needed for the gradient computation). The checkpoint read is done
  with ReadOnly status, which clones and re-inserts the handle.

  For require_grad = false, the fusion backend treats the tensor as a constant with
  no future autodiff use. The checkpoint read uses ReadWrite (draining the buffer
  to CPU), consuming the handle permanently.

  ---
  Workaround

  Do not use .no_grad() on parameters that must persist across checkpoint
  boundaries on the fusion backend. Instead, let gradients flow normally and
  strip the parameter's ParamId from GradientsParams before the optimizer step:

  fn step(&self, item: Input) -> TrainOutput<Output> {
      let out = self.forward_classification(item.tokens, item.labels);
      let mut grads = GradientsParams::from_grads(out.loss.backward(), self);
      if self.freeze_embeddings {
          for id in list_param_ids::<_, B>(&self.embedding) {
              let _ = grads.remove::<B::InnerBackend, 2>(id);
          }
      }
      TrainOutput { grads, item: out }
  }

  This keeps require_grad = true on the embedding weight, so the fusion backend
  maintains its handle across checkpoints. The optimizer never receives a gradient
  for the embedding, so the weights remain frozen.

  ---
  Expected behaviour

  no_grad() parameters should either:

  1. have their handles preserved across checkpoint serialisation on the fusion
  backend (using ReadOnly rather than ReadWrite during the drain), or
  2. be re-registered in the handle map after the checkpoint read completes.

  ---
  Environment

  burn        = "0.20.1"
  burn-train  = "0.20.1"
  burn-ir     = "0.20.1"
  backend     = wgpu (fusion enabled)
  OS          = Linux 6.17.0 x86_64

  ---

data.title: Global collective all-reduce fails on sequential calls due to hardcoded/reused transfer IDs
data.body:
> I used an LLM to help me write the issue below

**Describe the bug**

burn-collective's global all-reduce strategies (Tree, Centralized, Ring) use hardcoded or locally-scoped transfer IDs for the `TensorDataService`. When `all_reduce` is called multiple times in sequence (e.g., via `GradientsParams::all_reduce`, which iterates over each parameter tensor), the transfer IDs collide between calls, causing the data service to return the wrong tensor. This results in shape mismatches and panics.

Specifically:
- **Tree** ([`global/node/tree.rs`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/tree.rs)): hardcodes transfer IDs `0` and `1` at [L45](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/tree.rs#L45), [L66](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/tree.rs#L66), [L71](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/tree.rs#L71), [L87](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/tree.rs#L87)
- **Centralized** ([`global/node/centralized.rs`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/centralized.rs)): hardcodes transfer IDs `0` and `1` at [L42](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/centralized.rs#L42), [L62](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/centralized.rs#L62), [L68](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/centralized.rs#L68), [L73](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/centralized.rs#L73)
- **Ring** ([`global/node/ring.rs`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/ring.rs)): uses a local `transfer_counter` starting at `0` per call at [L83](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/src/global/node/ring.rs#L83), which resets on each invocation

Since the `TensorDataService` maintains a persistent WebSocket connection across calls, the second `all_reduce` call's `expose(..., 0.into())` collides with stale state from the first call. This causes nodes to download the wrong tensor, leading to `PeerSentIncoherentTensor` errors or panics in `broadcast_shape()` / `can_mut_broadcast()` due to shape mismatches.

**To Reproduce**

1. Set up a multi-node configuration with 2 nodes and a global orchestrator
2. Call `all_reduce` more than once in sequence on different tensors (this is what `GradientsParams::all_reduce` does — it iterates over all parameter gradients and calls `burn_collective::all_reduce` for each one)
3. The second `all_reduce` call panics with one of:
   - `PeerSentIncoherentTensor` — shape validation catches the wrong tensor
   - `index out of bounds: the len is 1 but the index is 1` — in `broadcast_shape()` when the downloaded tensor has fewer dimensions than expected

Minimal reproduction: modify the multinode-tests [`node.rs`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/multinode-tests/src/bin/node.rs#L146-L149) to call `all_reduce` twice with tensors of different shapes (e.g., first `[4, 8]`, then `[16]`). The second call will fail.

Note: the existing multinode-tests only call [`all_reduce` once per session](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-collective/multinode-tests/src/bin/node.rs#L148), which is why this wasn't caught.

**Expected behavior**

Sequential `all_reduce` calls should work correctly, each operating on its own tensor independently. This is required for [`GradientsParams::all_reduce`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/v0.20.1/crates/burn-optim/src/optim/grads.rs#L120-L155) to function, which iterates over all parameter gradients and calls `burn_collective::all_reduce` for each one — the primary integration point for DDP training with custom training loops.

**Suggested fix**

Use a monotonically increasing `AtomicU64` counter (stored on the `Node` struct or passed through the all-reduce functions) for transfer IDs, so each `expose`/`download_tensor` pair gets a globally unique ID across calls. The counter should persist across all `all_reduce` invocations for the lifetime of the collective session.

For tree.rs, instead of:
```rust
data_service.expose(result.clone(), 1, 0.into()).await;
// ...
.download_tensor(child_addr.clone(), 0.into())
```

Use something like:
```rust
let id = node.next_transfer_id(); // AtomicU64::fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst)
data_service.expose(result.clone(), 1, id.into()).await;
// ...
.download_tensor(child_addr.clone(), id.into())
```

**Desktop:**
- OS: Linux (Ubuntu 24.04)
- Burn version: 0.20.1
- Tested with both NdArray and CUDA backends — same behavior on both

**Additional context**

The local collective (intra-process, thread-based) handles sequential `all_reduce` calls correctly. The bug is specific to the global collective (inter-process, WebSocket-based) used for multi-node training.

This blocks any use of `GradientsParams::all_reduce` with the global collective, which means DDP training via the documented pattern (custom training loop + `GradientsParams::all_reduce`) cannot work in multi-node setups.

data.title: Audit slow unit tests that spawn excessive threads
data.body:
## Summary

Some unit tests in the workspace are unnecessarily slow, spawning thousands of threads or performing expensive operations that don't contribute to meaningful test coverage. These slow tests increase local development iteration time and CI costs.

## Examples

- Tests that spawn 1000+ threads to verify basic concurrent behavior
- GPU backend tests that attempt to initialize hardware on platforms where it's unavailable (e.g., CUDA tests on macOS)

## Suggestion

- Audit the test suite for tests with disproportionate resource usage relative to what they verify
- Reduce thread counts in concurrency tests to something reasonable (e.g., 4-8 threads instead of 1000s)
- Gate hardware-specific tests behind platform checks or feature flags
- Consider using `#[ignore]` for expensive integration-style tests so they don't run by default

Support signal processing operators: DFT, STFT, MelWeightMatrix, window functions
data.body:
### Feature description

Implement signal processing operators to improve coverage for ONNX models in Burn:
- Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__DFT.html)
- Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__STFT.html)
- MelWeightMatrix [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__MelWeightMatrix.html)
- HammingWindow [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__HammingWindow.html)
- HannWindow [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__HannWindow.html)
- BlackmanWindow [ONNX spec](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__BlackmanWindow.html)

These ops are currently missing, which blocks audio feature extraction and spectral model support when importing/exporting ONNX models via Burn.

### Feature motivation

Lack of signal processing ops prevents users from running common audio ML pipelines or speech models. Major ONNX models (e.g., for ASR, feature extraction) depend on these ops.

Supporting these ops would:
- Unblock model conversion for audio use-cases
- Enable end-to-end workflows involving audio or spectral models
- Close key compatibility gaps for potential adoption

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

- Template suggested: implement DFT, STFT, MelWeightMatrix, and common window functions per ONNX operator specs.
- Consider using existing Rust crates (e.g., rustfft for FFT-based ops)
- Review PyTorch or NumPy equivalents for reference implementations

Reference issue requesting these ops for Burn-ONNX importer: [tracel-ai/burn-onnx#161](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx/issues/161)

Thanks!

data.title: wgpu/Metal: naive_attention panics with shared memory overflow on Apple M3 Max
data.body:
## Describe the bug

Running a Depth-Anything-v2 (DINOv2 ViT-S/14) model with the wgpu backend on macOS/Metal panics in `naive_attention` -> `matmul` with:

```
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Unable to launch matmul with err:
Too many resources were requested during launch
Too much shared memory requested.
Requested 40960 bytes, maximum 32768 bytes available.
```

The model runs correctly on the ndarray backend. The panic comes from `cubek_matmul::launch::strategy::Strategy::launch_ref` at `cubek-matmul/src/launch/strategy.rs:454:22`.

This is likely related to #4492 (Q4S quantized matmul hits the same 32KB Metal shared memory limit), but this reproduces with standard f32 attention, not quantized matmul.

## To Reproduce

Using burn-onnx's model-check for Depth-Anything-v2:

```sh
cd crates/model-checks/depth-anything-v2
uv run get_model.py                                    # download model
cargo run --release --no-default-features --features wgpu  # panics
```

The model uses DINOv2 ViT-S/14 with 6 attention heads, 64-dim per head, and 1370 tokens (14x14 patches + CLS + registers). The attention call is `burn::tensor::module::attention(q, k, v, mask, scale)`.

Repository: https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx (branch `add-depth-anything-v2-check`, `crates/model-checks/depth-anything-v2/`)

## Expected behavior

The attention operation completes without panicking. The Metal GPU has 32KB shared memory; the matmul strategy should fall back to a kernel configuration that fits within this limit.

## Backtrace

```
thread 'main' panicked at cubek-matmul/src/launch/strategy.rs:454:22:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Unable to launch matmul with err: Too many resources were requested during launch
Too much shared memory requested.
Requested 40960 bytes, maximum 32768 bytes available.

stack backtrace:
   ...
   cubek_matmul::launch::strategy::Strategy::launch_ref
   burn_cubecl::kernel::matmul::base::matmul
   burn_cubecl::kernel::attention::naive_attention
   burn_cubecl::kernel::attention::attention
   <burn_cubecl::CubeBackend<R,F,I,BT> as burn_tensor::ops::ModuleOps<...>>::attention
   burn_tensor::tensor::module::attention
   depth_anything_v2::Model::forward
   depth_anything_v2_check::main
```

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.2 (Tahoe)
- GPU: Apple M3 Max (40 cores, Metal 4)
- Burn rev: `8bfa8f753bcccbbe59c489c9885a19ab4dd0c8f0`
- Backend: wgpu

## Additional context

The attention dimensions are: Q/K/V shape `[1, 6, 1370, 64]` (batch=1, heads=6, seq_len=1370, head_dim=64). The 40960 bytes requested (40KB) exceeds Metal's 32KB shared memory limit by 25%. A fallback to a smaller tile size or the naive path should handle this gracefully rather than panicking via `unwrap()`.

data.title: feat: add fold4d (col2im) operation as inverse of unfold4d
data.body:
## Summary

Burn has `unfold4d` (im2col) but no corresponding `fold4d` (col2im) operation. This is needed for implementing the ONNX `Col2Im` operator efficiently in burn-onnx, and is generally useful for any operation that needs to rearrange column blocks back into a multidimensional image (e.g., custom convolution implementations, attention mechanisms with spatial unfolding).

## Motivation

- PyTorch has both [`unfold`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Unfold.html) and [`fold`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Fold.html) as paired operations
- ONNX has both `Im2Col` (mapped to `unfold4d`) and `Col2Im` (no Burn equivalent)
- Without a native `fold4d`, burn-onnx has to generate per-element loop code with `slice`/`slice_assign`, which is orders of magnitude slower than a batched tensor operation (see tracel-ai/burn-onnx#169)
- Burn already has an internal `col2im` kernel in `burn-cubecl` for `conv_transpose2d`, but it's not exposed as a public tensor operation

## Proposed API

```rust
/// Rearranges columns back into a multidimensional image (inverse of unfold4d).
///
/// # Shapes
/// * x:      [batch_size, channels * kernel_h * kernel_w, num_blocks]
/// * returns: [batch_size, channels, height, width]
pub fn fold4d<B: Backend>(
    x: Tensor<B, 3>,
    output_size: [usize; 2],
    kernel_size: [usize; 2],
    options: UnfoldOptions,  // reuse existing options (stride, padding, dilation)
) -> Tensor<B, 4>
```

Mirrors PyTorch's `torch.nn.Fold` signature. Reuses the existing `UnfoldOptions` struct since the parameters are identical.

## Workaround / Default Implementation

A default implementation can be built using `scatter` with `IndexingUpdateOp::Add`:

1. Compute the index mapping from column positions to output image positions (accounting for stride, dilation, padding)
2. Use `Tensor::scatter(dim, indices, values, IndexingUpdateOp::Add)` to accumulate overlapping blocks into the output tensor

This avoids per-element loops entirely and works on any backend. Backend-specific implementations (e.g., reusing the existing cubecl `col2im` kernel) can override for better performance.

## Context

- burn-onnx PR implementing Col2Im: tracel-ai/burn-onnx#169
- Existing `unfold4d`: `crates/burn-tensor/src/tensor/module.rs`
- Existing internal `col2im` kernel: `crates/burn-cubecl/src/kernel/conv/conv_transpose2d/col2im.rs`

data.title: Benchmarking against (and with) MLX using Qwen3-0.6B
data.body:
Hi team!

I know there is discussion about Metal performance elsewhere, but I feel I have enough to justify a new topic. Feel free to close or move to a better place.

I have been working on [a serious implementation of Qwen3 using Burn](https://github.com/eidolons-ai/qwen3-burn) over the past week. I am a huge fan of the portability that Burn's architecture promises, as I anticipate the need for both training and inference in wildly different environments (datacenter, robust consumer hardware, and lightweight consumer hardware). However, my immediate target is Apple's M3/M4/M5 devices.

My implementation is fairly complete for text and vision variants, and applies most of the low-hanging optimizations. However, I continued to see performance (tok/s) nearly an order of magnitude worse than similar models running on the same hardware via LMStudio.

I wanted to see how much of this was due to inefficiencies in my implementation vs inherent limitations of WGPU/CubeCL.

I found burn-mlx and [updated it to work with burn 0.20](https://github.com/eidolons-ai/burn-mlx/tree/burn-0-20). While this appeared to be a very quick experiment by @ravituringworks (and probably not acheiving its full potential), I reasoned that any gains from it would imply direct opportunities for the WGPU/CubeCL backend.

I put together a [quick benchmarking tool](https://github.com/eidolons-ai/burn-mlx-benchmarks) comparing Burn (via both backends) and MLX (via both official front-ends).

Here are the benchmark results:

## Hardware

- **Chip**: Apple M4 Max
- **GPU Cores**: 40
- **Memory**: 128.0 GB
- **macOS**: 26.2

## Overall Decode Throughput

|-----------|----------:|-------:|--------:|
| burn-mlx  |      77.8 |   1.51 |       9 |
| burn-wgpu |      26.2 |   0.41 |       9 |
| mlx-lm    |     221.9 |   5.31 |       9 |
| mlx-swift |     220.7 |   5.72 |       9 |

## Speedup Ratios

- **mlx-lm** is **1.0x** faster than **mlx-swift**
- **mlx-lm** is **2.9x** faster than **burn-mlx**
- **mlx-lm** is **8.5x** faster than **burn-wgpu**

## Prefill Throughput (tokens/sec)

| Framework | Prompt |   Mean | Stddev |
|-----------|--------|-------:|-------:|
| burn-mlx  | long   | 59045.3 | 6677.42 |

---

In summary:

- mlx-swift used the least memory and acheived comparable throughput to mlx-lm
- mlx-lm (python) used 1.19x as much peak memory with comparable throughput to mlx-swift
- burn-mlx used 4.7x as much peak memory and ran about 2.8x slower
- burn-wgpu used 3.9x as much peak memory and ran about 8.5x slower

The difference between the first-party mlx-swft/mlx-lm frameworks and burn-mlx is probably a combination of poor tuning/optimization on my part in qwen3-burn and some limitations of burn itself.

The difference between burn-mlx and burn-wgpu *should* be pure opportunity for WGPU/CubeCL.

Happy to have any kind of discussion about this, or deep dive. Hopefully it's useful to see a real-world performance comparison.

data.title: Burn API limitations affecting ONNX operator coverage
data.body:
## Context

While expanding integration test coverage for [burn-onnx](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn-onnx), we identified several places where Burn's API limits what ONNX operators can support. These are not bugs in burn-onnx; they are upstream API gaps that prevent full ONNX spec compliance.

## 1. Pad: only supports last 2 spatial dimensions

ONNX `Pad` allows padding any dimension, but burn-onnx rejects models that pad batch or channel dimensions because Burn's pad API is designed for spatial (H, W) dimensions only.

**ONNX spec**: Pad can apply to any dimension of any rank tensor.
**Current behavior**: Error: `"Pad: padding will only be applied to the last two dimensions"`

## 2. Pad constant_value: float-only

ONNX `Pad` with `mode=constant` accepts int and bool constant values, but Burn only supports f32.

**ONNX spec**: `constant_value` can be any numeric or bool type matching the input tensor.
**Current behavior**: Error: `"only float values are currently supported for constant value"`

## 3. Resize: only Interpolate1d and Interpolate2d exist

ONNX `Resize` works on any spatial rank. Burn provides `Interpolate1d` (rank 3) and `Interpolate2d` (rank 4) modules, but nothing for 3D spatial data (rank 5).

**ONNX spec**: Resize supports 1D, 2D, and 3D spatial data.
**Current behavior**: Rank 5 (3D spatial) falls back to a slower runtime path rather than using a dedicated module.

## 4. LayerNorm: only normalizes the last dimension

ONNX `LayerNormalization` has an `axis` attribute that specifies the first normalization dimension; normalization spans `[axis, ..., rank-1]`. Burn's `LayerNorm` always normalizes the last dimension.

**ONNX spec**: `axis` can be any value in `[-rank, rank)`.
**Current behavior**: Error: `"LayerNorm: normalization is only supported on the last axis right now"`

## Impact

These limitations cause burn-onnx to reject valid ONNX models that use these features. They are documented in burn-onnx with TODO/FIXME comments referencing the Burn API as the blocker.

None of these are urgent, but addressing any of them would directly expand ONNX model compatibility.

data.title: ci: add wasm32 build check to prevent getrandom/no-std regressions in burn-wgpu
data.body:
## Summary

We recently fixed a wasm build failure caused by `getrandom` being pulled into `wasm32-unknown-unknown` builds through unconditional `std` feature propagation (see tracel-ai/burn-onnx#135, PR #4500). The fix required coordinated changes across three repos (cubecl, cubek, burn).

This type of regression is easy to reintroduce when updating dependency revs or adding new feature flags, since Cargo feature unification can silently re-enable `std` paths that pull in `getrandom`.

## Problem

The feature propagation chain that caused the failure:

```
burn-wgpu -> cubecl/std -> cubecl-common/std -> rand/thread_rng -> rand/sys_rng -> rand/getrandom -> getrandom 0.4
```

On `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `getrandom` requires an explicit backend (`wasm_js` or `wasm_wasi`). Without it, compilation fails with:

```
error: the wasm*-unknown-unknown targets are not supported by default, you may need to enable the "wasm_js" or "wasm_wasi" feature.
```

## Proposal

Add a CI job that runs a `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for a minimal crate that depends on `burn` with `webgpu` + `ndarray` features (the typical wasm configuration). This would catch any future dependency or feature flag change that reintroduces `getrandom` into the wasm build.

A simple smoke test like:

```sh
cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p some-wasm-example
```

would have caught the original regression immediately.

Refactor interpolate API to support both output_size and scale_factor in InterpolateOptions
data.body:
### Summary

The current `burn::tensor::module::interpolate` function requires `output_size` as a separate parameter:

```rust
pub fn interpolate<B>(
    x: Tensor<B, 4>,
    output_size: [usize; 2],  // Required separate param
    options: InterpolateOptions,  // Only contains mode
) -> Tensor<B, 4>
```

This differs from the higher-level Interpolate2d module which accepts either output_size or scale_factor via its config:

```rust

pub struct Interpolate2dConfig {
    pub output_size: Option<[usize; 2]>,
    pub scale_factor: Option<[f32; 2]>,
    pub mode: InterpolateMode,
}
```

###Motivation

This inconsistency causes code duplication. For example, in ONNX import (burn-onnx/src/burn/node/resize.rs), when handling runtime scales we
must manually compute output sizes in generated code:

```rust
let input_dims = input.dims();
let target_height = ((input_dims[2] as f64) * (scales_array[2] as f64)) as usize;
let target_width = ((input_dims[3] as f64) * (scales_array[3] as f64)) as usize;
burn::tensor::module::interpolate(input, [target_height, target_width], options)
```

This logic already exists in Interpolate2d::forward() via calculate_output_size().

### Proposed Change

Refactor InterpolateOptions to include sizing parameters:

```rust
pub struct InterpolateOptions {
    pub mode: InterpolateMode,
    pub output_size: Option<[usize; 2]>,
    pub scale_factor: Option<[f32; 2]>,
}


// New signature - output_size moves into options
pub fn interpolate<B>(
    x: Tensor<B, 4>,
    options: InterpolateOptions,
) -> Tensor<B, 4>

```

The function would compute the final output size internally when scale_factor is provided.

### Benefits

1. API consistency between low-level interpolate function and high-level Interpolate2d module
2. Reduced code duplication - size computation logic in one place
3. Simpler ONNX codegen - can pass scales directly without manual computation
4. Better ergonomics - builder pattern for options

### Breaking Change

This is a breaking change to interpolate's signature. Migration path:

// Before
interpolate(x, [224, 224], InterpolateOptions::new(mode))

// After
interpolate(x, InterpolateOptions::new(mode).with_output_size([224, 224]))

Related

- Context: PR fixing runtime scales support in ONNX Resize (issue tracel-ai/burn-onnx#3)
- File with TODO: crates/burn-onnx/src/burn/node/resize.rs:127-135

data.title: Refactor pool operations to use PoolOptions struct for functional-level asymmetric padding support
data.body:
### Summary

Pool operations (max_pool1d, max_pool2d, avg_pool1d, avg_pool2d) currently use individual parameters at the functional level, while asymmetric padding is handled at the module level. This is inconsistent with how convolution operations work after #4263.

### Current State

- Conv operations: Use ConvOptions<N> struct with padding_out field for asymmetric padding at the functional level
- Pool operations: Use individual parameters; asymmetric padding handled via explicit tensor.pad() at the module level only

### Proposed Change

1. Create a PoolOptions<N> struct (or separate MaxPoolOptions/AvgPoolOptions) similar to ConvOptions:

```rust 
pub struct PoolOptions<const N: usize> {
    pub kernel_size: [usize; N],
    pub stride: [usize; N],
    pub padding: [usize; N],
    pub padding_out: Option<[usize; N]>,
    pub dilation: [usize; N],  // for max_pool
    pub ceil_mode: bool,
    pub count_include_pad: bool,  // for avg_pool
}
```
2. Update functional pool APIs in burn-tensor/src/tensor/module.rs to use the options struct
3. Move asymmetric padding handling from module level to functional level

### Benefits

- Consistency with conv operations
- Users calling functional pool APIs directly get asymmetric padding support
- Cleaner API with fewer parameters

### Related

- PR #4263: Added asymmetric padding support for conv and pool operations (module-level for pools)

data.title: Missing 3D variants of operations
data.body:
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates -->

### Feature description

Medical images are often in 3D volume format. While you can use a 2D network to generate predictions, more often than not a model generally performs better when it is able to appreciate the larger out-of-plane spatial context.

A basic, but often used, architecture is the U-Net. So far it has been the dominant architecture for biomedical image segmentation since its introduction back in 2015. Creating a 3D U-Net requires 3D variants of the `MaxPool` layer, which burn unfortunately does not support yet. This prevents the further exploration of Burn for medical imaging related works.

I have not done an extensive search through all available layers, though I imagine there will be some more that only provide a 1D/2D implementation.

<!-- Describe the feature you'd like -->

### Feature motivation

See above. 3D models simply require 3D pooling operations to function properly.

<!-- Why do you want this? -->

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

I have looked through the code, and I don't _think_ I have identified any major issues that would prevent extending the 1D/2D variants into a third dimension. However, Burn's general architecture is significantly more complex than the software that I use in my research. Given that following the function calls seem to cross crate boundaries and I don't want to break anything, I am opening this issue first. Just in case someone already has a idea on how this can simply be added.

<!--
  How do you think we should implement this feature? 
  Things to address include:
    * Details of the technical implementation
    * Tradeoffs made in design decisions

data.title: [Feature] Implement Cross Attention and Windowed Attention
data.body:
This issue tracks support for two attention variants that are currently missing from Burn’s core modules:

Cross Attention (separate Query vs Key/Value)

Windowed/Local Attention (sliding window over the sequence)

Both are standard components in modern models, especially encoder–decoder architectures and long-sequence models.

Motivation

Cross Attention:
Required for any encoder–decoder architecture (e.g., T5, Whisper) and for conditioning mechanisms in generative models.

Windowed Attention:
Allows efficient long-sequence processing with complexity reduced from O(N²) to O(N × w).
Used in models like Mistral, long-form audio transformers, and streaming inference.

create Ord/CmpOps trait
data.body:
### Feature description

Take the existing Operations under Numeric that rely on Ording (such as clamp_min), and separate them into a new trait `OrdOps` or `CmpOps`

### Feature motivation

Some potential dtypes (such as complex numbers) don't form an ordered field ([relevant issue comment from num](https://github.com/rust-num/num/issues/321#issuecomment-321766313), so there isn't a correct way to order them. We could just make these methods panic if you call an op you can't do, but that seems less than ideal. The better solution (to me) is to separate out these ops so the available methods better reflects the underlying dtype.

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

- separate out everything that currently relies on elementwise comparison from numeric into a separate trait
- move the backend-side implementations to use the new trait.
- for the dtypes themselves, we can just make them panic in their cmp function if we consider direct scalar element comparisons something that is unlikely to happen in practice. Option 2 is to remove the constrain on Element and cmp out of the make_element macro

data.title: feat(dlpack): support `dlpack` for zero copy sharing
data.body:
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates -->

### Feature description

Support for consuming and exporting DLPack (`DLManagedTensor`) tensors. This would allow for zero-copy tensor sharing between Burn and other frameworks.

https://dmlc.github.io/dlpack/latest/

### Feature motivation

We're building libraries (https://metatensor.org/) that bridge multiple frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, and hopefully Burn via our Rust core). DLPack is the standard for zero-copy sharing.

Right now, moving a JAX tensor to Burn would require a `jax -> numpy (cpu) -> burn (gpu)` copy, or a `jax -> torch -> dlpack -> metatensor-torch` flow which is clumsy.

Direct DLPack support in Burn would let us (and others) build backends that can operate on JAX, PyTorch, or CuPy memory in-place, which is critical for performance.

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

This will be `unsafe` and highly backend-specific.

1. A new constructor on `burn-tensor` (or backend-specific tensor primitives) that can be initialized from a `DLManagedTensor` pointer.

2. This implementation would have to:

   * Read the `DLManagedTensor` struct (device type, device id, pointer, shape, strides).

   * Find the corresponding Burn `Device`.

   * **The hard part:** Use `unsafe` functions to wrap the existing native GPU buffer.

3. For `burn-wgpu`, this means using the underlying `wgpu` instance to import a native Vulkan `VkBuffer`, Metal `MTLBuffer`, etc. This seems related to the work discussed in `wgpu` for underlying API interop: https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/issues/4067

4. An equivalent `to_dlpack()` method would be needed to export a Burn tensor, which would package its own buffer handle into a `DLManagedTensor` struct with a valid deleter.

data.body:
**Describe the bug**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->
Wrapping inference code into a GStreamer element, I get a SIGBUS when loading the model, specifically when loading the record with the Recorder. It may have to do with threading, alignment, or exceeding allocated memory.

**To Reproduce**
<!-- 
 Steps to reproduce the behavior:
 1. Go to '...'
 2. Click on '....'
 3. Scroll down to '....'
 4. See error
-->
My element follows the structure of those in [gst-plugins-rs](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gst-plugins-rs/), and the error occurs regardless of where I try to load the model. I can try to make a minimal example, but the heart of the code is
```Rust
type MyBackend = Wgpu<f32, i32>;
let path = "path/to/model.mpk";
let device = WgpuDevice::Cpu;
let model = YOLOv9c::<MyBackend>::new(&device);
let recorder = burn::record::NamedMpkBytesRecorder::<burn::record::FullPrecisionSettings>::new();

// Error occurs here
let record: super::models::yolov9c::YOLOv9cRecord<MyBackend> = recorder.load(path.into(), &device).expect("Record file to exist.");

let model = model.load_record(record);
```
The exact same code works fine in a standalone non-GStreamer project.

**Expected behavior**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen. -->
A GStreamer element can successfully load and perform inference with the model.

**Screenshots**
<!-- If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem. -->

**Environment:**
 - OS: MacOS 15.6.1 
 - burn = { git = "https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn.git", features = ["wgpu"] }
 - cargo 1.89.0
 - cargo-c 0.10.14+cargo-0.89.0
 - GStreamer 1.26.4

**Additional context**
<!-- Add any other context about the problem here. -->
@sdroege is probably _the_ expert on the GStreamer side of things.
I haven't seen anything like this with tch or ort, possibly because they load the model via external libraries, rather than entirely in Rust in the element.

data.title: Implement optimized `fmod` operation for each backend, including burn-autodiff
data.body:
### Feature description

The current implementation of the `fmod` operation uses a default method  (https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/pull/3767) that may not be optimal for all backends. To improve performance and maintain consistency, we should implement specialized and optimized `fmod` methods tailored for each backend, including WGPU, Candle, and burn-autodiff.

### Feature motivation

Optimizing the `fmod` operation for each backend will improve performance, especially for workloads that rely heavily on modulo operations. This is particularly important for hardware-accelerated backends and also for the burn-autodiff backend where correct and efficient implementation is crucial for differentiable programming.

data.title: Relax Element Trait constraints
data.body:
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates -->

### Feature description

Somehow Relax the constraints for the Element trait to make it possible to define elements outside of burn-tensor

### Feature motivation

This came up primarily in #3608 in the process of trying to move complex element definitions to the crate `burn-complex`. The current major blocker is `ElementConversion`, ~~which has explicit function calls per primitive type~~ which relys on [`ToElement`](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/dd2a02905ea4a29ce2100e432e49d63b365546ab/crates/burn-tensor/src/tensor/element/cast.rs#L18) which has explict calls per type. This made it impossible to define an Element outside of `burn-tensor`. `ElementComparison` I believe depends on `ElementConversion`.

This currently blocks implementing `basicOps` (and thus quite a few other traits) on anything outside of burn tensor if the underlying dtype is not one of the already defined and supported primitives.

### (Optional) Suggest a Solution

completely spitballing:
- remove the ElementConversion, ElementComparision constraint from element. Make the basic ops that require members of a new trait (maybe `InteropOps`? lol). Really just shuffles the problem around though.
- find a way to rework the functions in element conversion to more like the signature of mem::transmute (i.e. `convert<E1,E2>(E1)-> E2` where both are Elements, but elements are not required to cover every implementor. The core primitives will cover all the other primitives in burn-tensor. You can have 2 variants, convert which is fast but unsafe in that it will panic if the required conversion method doesn't exists, and then `try_convert<E1,E2>(E1)-> Result<E2>` that will throw an error. This might be tricky converting external elements from burn-tensor elements since that would probably violate the orphan rule
- get rid of ElementConvert, and make the ops that currently require it require a From<E>, Into<E> specific to the 2 elements in question (the current element and  product element).

I'm open to other possibilities, and if there are downsides or tradeoffs to the above approaches I'm not seeing, please let me know.

data.title: Memory Hint: Improved Memory Management
data.body:
I believe we should try to improve our current memory management strategy for CubeCL backends. The goal is to reduce total memory usage by decreasing the amount of padding present in our memory pools and providing more information to our memory pools without requiring code changes for users.

The key idea here would be to add the concept of long-lived tensors and short-lived tensors. Parameters could be tagged as long-lived tensors, which would create a category of allocations with a fixed-size memory pool. These memory pools could have automatic deallocations based on padding in those memory pools, since they are only used by fixed tensors. Anyway, in most training and inference scenarios, model parameters are fixed, so deallocation would never happen. This optimization based on memory hints could be disabled for highly dynamic workloads to reduce the number of deallocations.

data.title: Complex Backend
data.body:
It's a bit early but could definitely use feedback on what works and doesn't in terms of the design

The goals are:
1. keep the implementation for complex numbers out of the core backend trait, and make it a decorator similar to autodiff.
2. don't constrain backends to a specific layout, but make it possible to define layout dependent shared behavior (like butterfly operations)
3. Don't make the ComplexBackend trait be a supertrait of Backend, while allowing ComplexBackend to be usable with backend (done)
4. implement split tensors which can work with any backend, and use flex-tensor for the first backend to support interleaved complex numbers

### Checklist

- [ ] Confirmed that `cargo run-checks` command has been executed.
- [ ] Made sure the book is up to date with changes in this PR.

### Related Issues/PRs

- continuation of #3330 
- would resolve #3265 
- required for #788 

### Changes

main changes in relation to the goals are:
1. made a new `burn-complex` crate that will house a lot of the shared definitions. I'm guessing most of the stuff other than the `ComplexTensorBackend` trait and dtype for complex numbers will be moved here
2. Added a dummy trait `ComplexLayout` that will be implemented on unit structs that indicate what type of complex layout is in use for an implementation, which allows implementors to define functions and traits only meant to be used for a specific data layout.

### Testing

TODO

### Notes

My current plan is to get all ops implemented for split and burn-flex, write test for the ops, and then once it's almost ready to merge, stash the ndarray implementation and make that a separate PR. It's just way easier to implement for flex. Ndarray macros do not spark joy.

data.title: Support custom gradient aggregation, surgery and RL signals
data.body:
<!-- Please search existing issues to avoid creating duplicates -->

### Feature description

Ability to do custom aggregation of gradients on layers;

Ability to append custom gradients to layers;

### Feature motivation

<!-- Why do you want this? -->

* This allows to implement gradient surgery
* This allows RL signals

### Suggested Solution

 [Here](https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/blob/main/crates/burn-autodiff/src/grads.rs#L67)  in the autodiff implementation we just add the gradients to each other from different branches, this is sum aggregation. 

We define trait: 

```rust

trait GradFold<B: Backend, const D: usize> {
    fn collect(&mut self, grad: Tensor<B,D>);

    fn finish(&self, &mut Ctx) -> Tensor<B,D>;

    // Optional
    fn clear(&mut self);
}
```

The register method of `Gradients` calls the collect on each register;  Then when the gradient is finally needed the finish is called and gradient is produced; We supply a default implementation with current behavior. 

The context is provided only for finish method: There we  formulate gradients for skip connections. Inside of context we thread layer labels to which we have skip connections. Any gradient which we set up this way ends up as a call to `collect`  of the `GradFold` trait. (Any additional info about the origin of gradient can also be supported.) 

The current decision is to draw the abstraction boundary at module level; so that it's not possible to send grads to something very far up in the data stream.... like posting gradients to a router layer outside of your current module.  Which raises consideration for adding a way to create opaque handles for `NodeId` s and to pass them around as needed;

Hence there're two possible `Ctx` APIs: one that sends grads by a token, which token  we then just get from a layers method. And the second, which allows to enumerate all labels in the module (I believe this can be done at compile time)  and send grads just there.

The implementations consideration is that any node of the tape now has a folder, even if it is the default one, so where would it go?

### Notes of aggregations

Some aggregation operations can be fully streaming, without internal buffers, the sum of gradient with the division on the number of the collected grads is example.

But for cases like gradient conflict estimation and resolution it may very well require buffering and running algorithms in finish stage;

And this raises a question of if the current JIT can efficiently support this?


<!--
  How do you think we should implement this feature?

    * Details of the technical implementation
    * Tradeoffs made in design decisions
    * Caveats and considerations for the future
-->

data.title: CubeCL memory allocator hits panic in on allocation overflow
data.body:
**Describe the bug**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->
Based on: https://github.com/tracel-ai/burn/issues/3465

(This is being opened as a new issue to provide additional context regarding the failure of the autotuning process due to OOM).

Running the resnet-burn fine-tuning example from [tracel-ai/models](https://github.com/tracel-ai/models) with --features wgpu can panic during conv autotuning:
`No pool handles allocation of size <N>
`
This comes from CubeCL’s memory allocator (the pinned commit that specifies the CubeCL version), when a kernel candidate requests more memory than any pool allows.

The panic aborts the entire autotuner run instead of skipping the failed candidate and testing others.

This prevents Burn from gracefully handling OOM-like conditions and causes the entire process to terminate.
**To Reproduce**

 Steps to reproduce the behavior:
 1. Clone [tracel-ai/models](https://github.com/tracel-ai/models)
 2. From models/resnet-burn, run with a high enough batch size:
`cargo run -r --example finetune --features wgpu
```
 3. Observe panic from: 
`=== PANIC ===
A fatal error happened, you can check the experiment logs here => '/tmp/resnet-finetune/experiment.log'
=============

thread 'main' panicked at cubecl-runtime/src/memory_management/memory_manage.rs:341:32:
No pool handles allocation of size 411041792
```

**Expected behavior**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen. -->

- The allocator should return an error (e.g. IoError::BufferTooBig, as handled in the main branch of cubecl) instead of panicking.
- The conv autotuner should catch OOM/oversize errors for one candidate and continue with the remaining ones.
- Only if all candidates fail should the autotune step error out.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - Device: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 (Laptop/PC GPU)
 - OS: Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS (WSL2) / Windows 11 Host
 - Browser: N/A
 - Version: CUDA 12.2, NVIDIA Driver 535.xx

**Additional context**
<!-- Add any other context about the problem here. -->
The pinned CubeCL commit in burn uses:
```.find(|p| p.max_alloc_size() >= size)
.unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("No pool handles allocation of size {size}"));
```
CubeCL’s main branch now replaces this with an error return:
```
.find(|p| p.max_alloc_size() >= size)
.ok_or(IoError::BufferTooBig(size))?;

```

data.title: Slow metal performance
data.body:
**Describe the bug**

I'm getting about 0.03 token/second running qwen2 0.5b with the metal backend on a macbook m2 8gb ram. I get about 20 tokens/second running with the candle cpu backend. The output from the generation also isn't right.
 
I get the same behaviour running with fp16 and fp32

**To Reproduce**

1) Clone https://github.com/piedshag/lm
2) Run `cargo run --release --features metal`

**Expected behavior**

I would expect metal to be faster than the cpu backend.
